title: Seven hours since the tablets
objective: Manage acetaminophen overdose: establish the time of ingestion, check a level timed to the nomogram, give N-acetylcysteine early, and watch for liver and kidney failure

sources.cite: Adult critical care nursing certification exam handbook and test plan: toxic ingestions within the multisystem category
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/ccrn.ts), which read the handbook 2026-10-31, not re-read: toxic ingestions within the multisystem category is tested. Scope only.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.cite: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acetaminophen Poisoning (O'Malley GF, O'Malley R; reviewed April 2025, updated March 2026)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes: stage I (first 24 hours) brings 'Anorexia, nausea, vomiting', and 'Mild poisoning may not cause symptoms'; the Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies to a single acute ingestion with levels 'measured >= 4 hours after ingestion', and 'Serum levels drawn before 4 hours may not represent peak levels'; acetylcysteine 'is most effective if given within 8 hours of acetaminophen ingestion', and is given until toxicity is ruled out when it is uncertain; liver tests and, in suspected severe poisoning, prothrombin time; stage III at 72-96 hours brings the peak of AST, ALT, bilirubin and INR. No dose is used in the case.

brief.situation: 08:00 in a medical ICU. You are Mr. Tan's nurse. He is 31, admitted from the emergency department at 07:30 for monitoring after taking a large number of extra-strength acetaminophen tablets over half an hour for a dental abscess, not knowing the daily limit. He feels nauseated and otherwise well.
handover: The emergency department note says 'ingestion about 01:00?' and 'acetaminophen level drawn 05:00, pending'.
Order: the ordered IV acetylcysteine protocol 'if the level is above the treatment line'. Liver tests and INR have not been sent.
Unit policy: the nurse plots a timed level on the nomogram and starts an acetylcysteine order as soon as its condition is met, then tells the intensivist.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Liver injury accrues the longer acetylcysteine is delayed. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It stops accruing once acetylcysteine is running. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

The 8-hour mark after a 01:00 ingestion falls at 09:00; 08:59 is the authored last moment to start inside it. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Acetylcysteine within 20 minutes of the level being plotted (authored target). FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The intensivist told within 5 minutes of plotting the level (unit practice).
The intensivist reviews him with the liver tests: about 30 min.

why.question: Why does the time of ingestion matter, what does the level mean, and how soon must he be treated?

parts.label: Time and level
parts.criteria: The nomogram needs a single acute ingestion and a known time; a level drawn 4 hours or more after it is plotted; his 4-hour level is above the treatment line; looking well early is typical and reassures nothing.
parts.modelAnswer: The nomogram only works with a known time and a single ingestion, so I pinned it at 01:00. His level was drawn 4 hours later and plots well above the treatment line. Feeling fairly well now doesn't mean much: early symptoms are often mild.

parts.label: How soon
parts.criteria: Acetylcysteine now, ideally within 8 hours of ingestion (09:00); does not wait for a repeat level; baseline liver tests, INR and kidney function; tells the intensivist.
parts.modelAnswer: Start the acetylcysteine now; it works best within 8 hours, and that's 09:00. I won't wait for a repeat level. Send baseline liver tests, INR and creatinine and tell the intensivist.

noProgress.rationale: A toxic acetaminophen level untreated past 8 hours is harm here.

expertPath.text: Pin the time of ingestion: about 01:00, a single acute ingestion.
Plot the 05:00 level: well above the treatment line. The 8-hour mark is 09:00.
Start the ordered acetylcysteine; send liver tests, INR, creatinine; tell the intensivist; document.

windowLost.headline: Window lost
windowLost.body: Acetylcysteine is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion. With a level above the treatment line, start it now; a repeat level or a well-looking patient is no reason to wait.

protected.headline: Treated in time

time_up.headline: Untreated
time_up.body: A level above the line needs acetylcysteine before the 8-hour mark.

scoring.modelReasoning: The nomogram applies to a single acute ingestion with a known time, using a level drawn 4 hours or more after it. Mr. Tan took the tablets between 00:45 and 01:15, so the 05:00 level is a 4-hour level, and it plots well above the treatment line. He looks fairly well, which is typical early and reassures nothing. Acetylcysteine is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion, which is 09:00, so start the ordered protocol now rather than waiting for a repeat level, send baseline liver tests, INR and kidney function, tell the intensivist, and document the times. Liver injury peaks at 3 to 4 days, so the monitoring continues.

choices.label: From 4 hours after a single acute ingestion

nomoQ.explain: The nomogram applies to a single acute ingestion with levels measured 4 hours or more after it; earlier levels may not represent the peak.
